# Fitting the best straight line {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(webexercises)
library(here)
```

This page summarises what we covered in the first hour of the
regression session. Use it for revision; the full activities were
worked through in class.

**Progression:** draw a line → measure how far each point misses it →
choose the line that misses least → ask how precisely the slope is
known → check whether a straight line is good enough → predict with
the right interval.

## From labels to measurements {#sec-reg-labels}

In Session 4 the predictor was a label: Cross (x = 0) and Self
(x = 1). The slope, −2.62 inches, was the difference between the two
group means, and the line did not mean that height changes gradually
between the groups. This session's predictor is wood density, a
measurement, and the response is timber hardness on the Janka scale.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
When x is a measurement, the slope is the change in y for a one-unit
increase in x. Values between the observed densities now mean
something, so the line can be used for prediction within the range of
the data. The model is fitted with the same function as in Session 4:
`lm(hardness ~ dens)`.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** A line has a slope of 0.5 hundred Janka
units per unit of density. A sample of density 50 is expected to be
`r fitb(5)` hundred Janka units harder than a sample of density 40.
:::

## The best line by eye {#sec-reg-eye}

Everyone worked from the same 8 of the 36 samples, with hardness in
hundreds of Janka units and both values rounded:

| Sample                 | 1   | 2   | 3    | 4    | 5    | 6    | 7    | 8    |
|------------------------|-----|-----|------|------|------|------|------|------|
| Density (x)            | 25  | 30  | 39   | 43   | 48   | 53   | 60   | 66   |
| Hardness (y, hundreds) | 4.8 | 5.9 | 10.7 | 12.7 | 17.6 | 18.8 | 19.4 | 32.6 |

Each student drew a line by eye, read two points on it to calculate its
slope, b = (y~2~ − y~1~) ÷ (x~2~ − x~1~), and intercept,
a = y~1~ − b × x~1~, then calculated the fitted value, residual and
squared residual for each sample. Partners compared their sums of
squared residuals (SSR) to see whose line missed the points least.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reg-card
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The 8 samples from the card, with the least-squares line. Dashed segments are the residuals: the vertical distances from each point to the line."

card <- tibble(
  sample = 1:8,
  dens = c(25, 30, 39, 43, 48, 53, 60, 66),
  hardness_100 = c(4.8, 5.9, 10.7, 12.7, 17.6, 18.8, 19.4, 32.6)
)

card_fit <- lm(hardness_100 ~ dens, data = card)

broom::augment(card_fit, data = card) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dens, y = hardness_100)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(card_fit)[1], slope = coef(card_fit)[2],
              linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = dens, yend = .fitted), linetype = "dashed",
               colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sample), nudge_x = -1.5, nudge_y = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(20, 70)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 35)) +
  labs(x = "Wood density", y = "Janka hardness (hundreds)")
```

The residuals of a well-placed line add up to roughly zero, so their
sum cannot tell two reasonable lines apart. Squaring each residual
before adding makes every miss count, and makes large misses count
most. Samples 7 and 8 have the largest residuals of the least-squares line
in @fig-reg-card, and together they contribute about 87% of its SSR.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
A residual is the vertical distance from a point to the line: observed
minus fitted, e = y − ŷ. Points above the line have positive residuals
and points below it have negative ones. The method of **least squares**
chooses the line with the smallest possible sum of squared residuals.
This is what `lm()` does.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** A line has a = −12 and b = 0.6. For
sample 5 (density 48, hardness 17.6), the fitted value is
`r fitb(16.8)` and the residual is `r fitb(0.8)`.

`r hide("Explanation")`
ŷ = −12 + 0.6 × 48 = 16.8, so e = 17.6 − 16.8 = 0.8. The point lies
just above the line.
`r unhide()`
:::

## The computer's line {#sec-reg-ls}

R fitted the least-squares line to the same 8 samples:

| Intercept (a) | Slope (b) | SSR  |
|---------------|-----------|------|
| −12.06        | 0.602     | 52.7 |

No line drawn by eye can have a smaller SSR on these 8 samples, because
least squares finds the minimum. R also fitted the model to all 36
samples, with hardness in its original units:

| Term        | Estimate | Standard error |
|-------------|----------|----------------|
| (Intercept) | −1160.50 | 108.58         |
| dens        | 57.51    | 2.28           |

Multiplying the least-squares slope for the 8 samples (0.602 hundred
Janka units) by 100 gives 60.2 Janka units per unit of density, close
to the 57.51 from all 36 samples. The intercept,
−1160.5, is the predicted hardness at a density of zero: an impossible
value, because the densities in the data run from 24.7 to 69.1.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
The intercept is the height of the line at x = 0. When x = 0 is far
outside the data, the intercept is not a value that could occur, but it
is still needed to position the line. Subtracting the mean of x from
every value, called **centring**, moves x = 0 to the middle of the
data, so the intercept becomes the prediction at the mean of x. You do
this in hour 2.
:::

## How precisely is the slope known? {#sec-reg-precision}

The slope from all 36 samples has t = 57.51 ÷ 2.28 ≈ 25.2. A straight
line estimates two coefficients, so the residual degrees of freedom
are 36 − 2 = 34, and the 95% multiplier is 2.03. The 95% confidence
interval for the slope is 57.51 ± 2.03 × 2.28, which is 52.9 to 62.1
Janka units per unit of density.

We then discussed a classmate's claim that a t this large proves that
denser wood is harder *because* it is denser.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
As in Session 4, t = estimate ÷ SE, and the p-value is read from the
t-distribution. With two coefficients, df = n − 2. The 95% confidence
interval is the estimate ± multiplier × SE. A regression of
observational data measures association: the t for the slope is
exactly the t from a test of the correlation between the two
variables. An argument about cause has to come from elsewhere, such as
knowledge of wood structure or an experiment.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** A straight-line regression is fitted to
50 observations. The residual degrees of freedom are `r fitb(48)`.
:::

## Is a straight line good enough? {#sec-reg-residuals}

A residual plot puts the predictor on the x-axis and the residuals on
the y-axis. Each student plotted the 8 residuals from their own line,
then matched four residual plots, similar to those in
@fig-reg-patterns, to the problem each one shows.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reg-patterns
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Four residual plots, each from a different simulated data set. P: a curved relationship. Q: spread increasing with x. R: even scatter, so a straight line is adequate. S: one unusual point."

set.seed(11)
x_vals <- sort(runif(40, 20, 70))

tibble(
  x = rep(x_vals, 4),                                      # was: x = rep(x, 4)
  plot = rep(paste("Plot", c("P", "Q", "R", "S")), each = 40),
  residual = c(
    0.012 * (x_vals - 45)^2 - 2.5 + rnorm(40, 0, 0.9),     # was: (x - 45)^2
    rnorm(40) * (0.15 + 0.07 * (x_vals - 20)),             # was: (x - 20)
    rnorm(40, 0, 1.6),
    replace(rnorm(40, 0, 1.1), 28, 7.2)
  )
)|>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ plot) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "Residual")
```

With only 8 points, it was hard to say whether any student's sketch
showed a real pattern. Random scatter in a small sample can look like a
curve or a fan.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
A linear model assumes that the relationship is a straight line, that
the residuals have the same spread at every value of x, that they are
roughly normally distributed, and that the observations are
independent. A residual plot checks the first two at a glance. Patterns
are hard to judge with few points; in hour 2 you check the residuals of
all 36 samples.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** Which plot in @fig-reg-patterns suggests
that the residuals do not have the same spread at every value of x?
`r mcq(c("Plot P", answer = "Plot Q", "Plot R", "Plot S"))`
:::

## Predicting a new sample {#sec-reg-predict}

The model fitted to all 36 samples predicts a hardness of 1715 for a
density of 50, with two different 95% intervals:

| Interval                                | Lower | Upper |
|-----------------------------------------|-------|-------|
| Confidence interval for the mean        | 1650  | 1780  |
| Prediction interval for one new sample  | 1337  | 2093  |

The prediction interval is much wider because a single new sample
varies around the line as well as the line itself being uncertain. For
a density of 22 the model predicts a hardness of 105, with a 95%
confidence interval of −22 to 231. That prediction is untrustworthy for
two reasons: 22 lies below the lowest density in the data, and the
interval includes impossible negative values.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
A **confidence interval** describes uncertainty about the mean of y at
a given x. A **prediction interval** describes where a single new
observation is likely to fall, so it also includes the scatter of
individual points around the line and is always wider. Predicting
outside the range of x in the data is **extrapolation**: the model has
no information there, and a straight line can produce impossible
values.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** A timber merchant wants the likely
hardness of one new plank with a density of 50. Which interval should
you give them?
`r mcq(c("The confidence interval", answer = "The prediction interval"))`
:::

## Predictions for hour 2 {#sec-reg-predictions}

At the end of the hour you wrote predictions on Part G of the
worksheet: the SSR that R would calculate for your own line, and which
of plots P to S the residuals of all 36 samples would most resemble.
Bring them, and your residual table and sketch, to hour 2. Each one is
tested there.

## Exit ticket {#sec-reg-exit}

The question posed at the end of the hour:

> Two timber samples differ in density by 10 units. Using the slope and
> the 95% confidence interval from all 36 samples, how much harder do
> you expect the denser sample to be on average? Give the interval as
> well.
